title: The Kingdom and the Knot
hookLine: the book ends back in the forest: the goddess asks a king and a merchant what each one wants
carry: bhukti and mukti: she grants the world and freedom
tomorrow: in Bengal, the warrior goddess comes home as a daughter. why?

lines: WHAT WILL THEY DO WITH IT?
cards: Remember the forest? A king who'd lost his kingdom, a merchant thrown out by his own family, both asking a sage why knowing doesn't help. Year four began with them.
Every story since, the sleeping Vishnu, the buffalo, Kali, Raktabija, Shumbha, has been the sage's answer to the king's question: who is this goddess? Now the battles are done.
One more hymn, one more promise, and then the book walks back into the forest, to the two men who were listening the whole time.

teach.b: In the eleventh chapter, after Shumbha falls, the gods praise her once more, calling her Narayani, and ask her to be gracious to the whole world. Her promise is bigger than before.

teach.h: WHENEVER TROUBLE RISES, I WILL COME.
teach.b: In paraphrase: whenever trouble rises from the demons, I will come down and destroy the enemy. She even names future appearances.

In one, during a terrible drought, she will feed the world with plants grown from her own body, and be called Shakambhari, she who bears the greens. In the twelfth chapter she tells what hearing this story brings.
Then the thirteenth, the last. Medhas finishes: this is the goddess I told you of. She draws you into confusion, and she can set you free.

teach.h: AN EARTH IMAGE BY A RIVER.
teach.b: So the king and the merchant go to a riverbank, make an image of the goddess out of earth, and worship her there a long time. She appears and asks each what he wants.

teach.h: A KINGDOM, AND FREEDOM FROM I AND MINE.
teach.b: The king asks for his kingdom back in this life, and a kingdom that won't be lost in the next. She grants it. The merchant, who couldn't stop worrying about the family that threw him out, asks for something else.
In paraphrase: the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine. She grants that too. Two men, two requests, and the text doesn't rank them.

teach.h: BHUKTI AND MUKTI: THE WORLD, AND FREEDOM.
teach.b: Hindus have a pair of words for it: bhukti, the good things of this world, and mukti, freedom. The goddess is praised as the giver of both. The book that began with two worries ends with two answers.

how: Some Hindus who recite the whole Devi Mahatmya finish with the thirteenth chapter's boons to the king and the merchant, and the eleventh chapter's hymn to Narayani is also chanted on its own.

o: a king's prayer to win back his lost kingdom
the hymn that names the goddess Narayani
the glory of the goddess, from forest to riverbank

games.q: the last pages — tap the pairs.
p: the name the gods praise her by
feeds the world with greens in a drought
asks for knowledge that cuts I and mine

s: the book ends with the death of Shumbha
it goes back to the forest frame: the king and the merchant worship the goddess and receive her boons.
the king and the merchant ask for the same thing
the king asks for his kingdom; the merchant asks for the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine.
the goddess grants worldly gifts as well as spiritual ones
she gives the king his kingdom and the merchant liberating knowledge: bhukti and mukti, the world and freedom.

games.q: you're the merchant. your family threw you out, and you couldn't stop worrying about them. now the goddess stands in front of you and asks what you want. what do you ask?
o: my wealth and my family back.
the knowledge that cuts the knot of I and mine.
games.why: the merchant asks for the knowledge that frees him from I and mine. the king asks for his kingdom. the goddess grants both.

practice: Let the goddess's question sit quietly in you: what do you want?
Let the first, practical answer come, the kingdom, and notice it kindly; then wait a little longer for a quieter one underneath, the merchant's kind, without choosing between them.
If you pray, bring both before the goddess or God in your own words; if not, let the question rest on the breath.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. The glory of the goddess, read whole: two men in a forest who can't let go, and at the end, each asking her for what he wants.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Nārāyaṇī, a name of the goddess in the gods' hymn of the eleventh chapter.

carryVoice: Your line: bhukti and mukti, she grants the world and freedom. She asked each man what he wanted, and granted both. Ten days, one book, read whole.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 11 (the hymn to Narayani; the promise to return)
